entries.query: Az osszes mindent tesztelj le Peldaul az autonom munka az fixen tudom hogy max 1 perc utan calasz nelkul egyszeruen eldobja es kesz leal Normalisan eros agentic loop nak kene lennie es valosan akar 20 oran at autonom modon dolgoznia az agent swarmnak akkor is ha user be zarja az appot
entries.answer:
Röviden: a csatolt kód jelenlegi formában nem egy valóban hosszú életű, 20 órás autonóm worker-architektúra, hanem egy Flask folyamatból indított háttérszálas megoldás, ezért az általad leírt “egyszer csak eldobja” jelenség teljesen reális.  A legnagyobb gondok a heartbeat nélküli SSE stream, a `daemon=True` háttérszálak, a robot 60 lépéses plafonja, az 5 perces human wait, valamint az, hogy a futás ugyan perzisztens job store-ra támaszkodik, de a tényleges végrehajtás még mindig az alkalmazásfolyamathoz van kötve.[1]

## Hol szakad el

Az `/api/agent` és az `/api/chat` végpont új jobot hoz létre, majd `threading.Thread(..., daemon=True)` szálon indítja el a `runagentjob(...)` futást, tehát a munka nem külön worker processben vagy queue-rendszerben él, hanem a webszerver folyamatának mellékterméke.  Ugyanezek a végpontok SSE választ adnak vissza, ahol a generátor egyszerűen `liveq.get()`-re vár, és nincs beépített keepalive vagy heartbeat esemény, ezért ha egy ideig nincs új chunk, a kliens, proxy vagy böngésző könnyen idle timeoutnak veheti a kapcsolatot.  Emiatt az általad tapasztalt nagyjából egyperces “csendes ledobás” sokkal inkább stream-életciklus hiba, mint valódi autonóm logikai döntés.[1]

## Miért nem 20 órás még

A kódban több kemény plafon is látszik: `MAXTOOLROUNDS = 20`, `ROBOTMAXSTEPS = 60`, `ROBOTHUMANTIMEOUT = 300`, a `RobotStore.ROBOTTTL = 3600`, és az InstaVM oldalán is vannak rövid alapértelmezett életciklusok, például `createvm(..., vmlifetimeseconds=300)` vagy session timeout paraméterek.  Ezek együtt nem egy “napokig magától dolgozó swarm” profilját adják, hanem egy rövid életű, interaktív, felügyelet melletti agentet.  Az is fontos, hogy bár van `PersistentJobStore`, `runningjobs()` és `resumeinterruptedjobs()`, ez inkább újraindítás utáni mentés-visszaállítás, nem pedig valódi, processztől független, folyamatos háttérfutás.[1]

## Mi kell az erős agentic loophoz

A mostani kódban már megvannak azok az elemek, amelyekre lehet építeni: van perzisztens job store, van restartkori `resumeinterruptedjobs()`, és az InstaVM réteg tud aszinkron execute-ot, volume-okat, checkpointokat, webhooks-ot és külön session/VM kezelést.  Ami hiányzik, az a végrehajtás leválasztása a Flask request-ciklusáról: a munka ne `daemon` threadben fusson, hanem dedikált workerben, queue-val, lease/heartbeat mechanizmussal, per-step állapotgéppel és időszakos checkpointtal. Egy erős megoldásban a UI csak néző és vezérlő lenne, a tényleges agent pedig külön szolgáltatásként élne tovább akkor is, ha a felhasználó bezárja az appot vagy megszakad az SSE kapcsolat.[1]

## Mit javítanék azonnal

Első lépésként az SSE streamekbe 10–20 másodpercenként heartbeat eseményt tennék, hogy az idle kapcsolat ne haljon meg csendben, mert most az endpoint csak akkor küld bármit, ha új esemény érkezik a queue-ból.  Második lépésként kivenném a `daemon=True` modellt, és a `runagentjob(...)`/robot futásokat külső workerre tenném, mert a jelenlegi forma ugyan háttérbe teszi a munkát, de még mindig a webfolyamat élettartamától függ.  Harmadik lépésként minden hosszú feladatot explicit állapotokra bontanék — `queued`, `running`, `blocked_human`, `checkpointed`, `resuming`, `completed`, `failed` — és minden állapotváltást adatbázisba írnék, hogy 20 órás futásnál se “memóriából” éljen a rendszer.[1]

## Mit érdemes végigpróbálni

A jelenlegi kód alapján a legfontosabb tesztek ezek lennének: SSE idle 90 percig válasz nélkül, böngészőtab bezárása közben futó job, teljes frontend újratöltés, backend process kill és restart közbeni resume, hálózati szakadás utáni reconnect, emberi inputra váró robot 5 percen túli helyzete, 60 lépésnél megálló browser robot, valamint több párhuzamos swarm futás a `SWARMSEMLIMIT = 4` mellett.  Ezen felül külön soak test kellene 6 órára, 12 órára és 20 órára, mert itt már nem az algoritmus a fő ellenség, hanem az időzítés, a kapcsolat-élettartam, az erőforrás-újrafoglalás és a checkpoint-visszatöltés fegyelme. A legjobb következő irány egy külön worker + queue + heartbeat + checkpoint alapú átépítés, mert enélkül ez stabil interaktív agent lehet, de nem megbízható, “bezárom az appot és másnap is megy” swarm rendszer.[1]

Akarod, hogy a következő üzenetben adjam a konkrét refaktor tervet fájl- és függvényszintű bontásban?

entries.answer:
1. `validateenv()` only prints a warning for missing `CEREBRASAPIKEY`, `EXAAPIKEY`, `REQUESTLYAPIKEY`, and `INSTAVMAPIKEY` instead of failing startup, so the process can enter a half-initialized state and then fail later in unrelated execution paths.[1]

2. `cerebrasclient`, `requestyclient`, and `requestyasyncclient` are initialized with placeholder fallback keys, which means configuration errors are converted into delayed runtime failures instead of a deterministic boot-time stop.[1]

3. `runagentpipeline(...)` is wrapped in `while True` with retry-and-sleep behavior on exceptions, so a permanent bug can spin forever without a terminal failure state or retry ceiling.[1]

4. `generatescript(...)` also uses `while True` and rotates through models indefinitely, so a non-recoverable prompt/model incompatibility can loop forever and never surface as a hard failure.[1]

5. `executetaskwithretry(...)` contains an unbounded `while not success` loop, so a task can continue retrying forever even when the failure mode is permanent rather than transient.[1]

6. `retryasync(...)` is an unbounded retry helper with `while True`, so any caller using it on a deterministic failure path can block a workflow forever instead of terminating predictably.[1]

7. Worker launch paths use `threading.Thread(..., daemon=True)`, which means in-flight agent work can be dropped abruptly when the parent process exits, restarts, or crashes.[1]

8. `ROBOTMAXSTEPS = 60` hard-limits browser/computer-use autonomy, so long workflows are guaranteed to stop even if the task is still progressing correctly.[1]

9. `ROBOTHUMANTIMEOUT = 300` imposes a five-minute human gate timeout, which makes long unattended runs fail or stall instead of remaining durable.[1]

10. `RobotStore.ROBOTTTL = 3600` expires robot state after one hour, which is incompatible with any design goal resembling very long autonomous execution.[1]

11. `PersistentJobStore.JOBTTL = 86400` imposes a one-day retention cutoff, so long jobs and restart recovery are bounded by TTL rather than actual completion state.[1]

12. `cleanupoldtaskdirs()` deletes task directories older than 86400 seconds based on filesystem mtime, which can remove still-relevant artifacts for long jobs whose directory contents are no longer being touched.[1]

13. `InstaVMManager.req(...)` creates a fresh `httpx.Client` for every request, which throws away connection pooling and increases latency and resource overhead across heavily used API paths.[1]

14. `GitHubManager.req(...)` repeats the same per-request `httpx.Client` creation pattern, producing the same avoidable performance penalty and connection churn.[1]

15. Both manager `req(...)` methods normalize errors into plain dictionaries instead of raising typed exceptions, which pushes error checking onto every caller and makes silent mishandling much more likely.[1]

16. `cleanupoldtaskdirs()` catches `Exception` and silently `pass`es, so filesystem permission problems, partial deletions, and unexpected OS errors are suppressed with no remediation path.[1]

17. The codebase repeatedly uses broad `except Exception` blocks around critical orchestration paths, which collapses programming bugs, infrastructure faults, and bad inputs into the same retry flow and makes diagnosis materially worse.[1]

18. `toposorttasks(...)` treats a dependency cycle as executable by doing `if not batch: batch = list(remaining)`, so invalid DAGs are not rejected and are instead executed in dependency-violating order.[1]

19. Because `toposorttasks(...)` does not raise on cycles or unsatisfied dependencies, downstream execution can proceed with logically impossible task ordering while appearing successful at the scheduler level.[1]

20. `phaseswarm(...)` stores every task result into `taskcontext` using `taskcontext[r["id"]] = r.get("message","")` without checking `status`, so failed task outputs contaminate the context for dependent tasks.[1]

21. The context passed into later swarm tasks is just a joined string of prior task messages, which loses structured result semantics and makes dependency consumption brittle and error-prone.[1]

22. `phaseswarm(...)` uses `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` and then converts exceptions into synthetic error dictionaries, which prevents hard scheduling failures from aborting the graph even when continuation is invalid.[1]

23. `parseexecresult(stdout)` first tries the whole string, then the last non-empty line, then a greedy regex over `r"{.*status.*}"` with `re.DOTALL`, which can swallow too much text and parse the wrong JSON object from noisy output.[1]

24. The greedy JSON extraction strategy in `parseexecresult(...)` is especially fragile when stdout contains multiple JSON-like blocks, because it can bind from the first `{` to the last `}` and return the wrong slice.[1]

25. `parsessechunk(chunk)` only handles chunks starting with `data:` and ignores the broader SSE framing rules such as multiline `data:` payloads and other fields, so valid SSE messages can be misparsed or lost.[1]

26. In `agenticstream(...)`, tool call arguments are parsed with `json.loads(tc.function.arguments or "")`, so an empty argument string becomes a JSON decode failure instead of a valid empty-args case.[1]

27. The fallback `best = max(memberresponses, key=lambda r: len(r[1]))` chooses the longest response rather than the most correct or highest-confidence one, which is a quality bug in the synthesis failure path.[1]

28. `workermodelfortaskid(taskid)` assigns models by `md5(taskid) % len(SWARMMODELS)`, so model selection depends on an arbitrary identifier rather than task characteristics, capability fit, cost profile, or observed performance.[1]

29. Because `workermodelfortaskid(...)` keys on task ID instead of content, the same logical task can land on different models across runs solely due to a different generated identifier.[1]

30. `dispatchcouncilsync(...)` and `dispatchswarmsync(...)` duplicate nearly the same thread/queue orchestration code, which increases maintenance drift risk and makes future fixes easy to apply inconsistently.[1]

31. The history persistence block that appends user/assistant messages and calls `setsessionhistory(...)` appears duplicated across normal and fast pipeline branches, which is needless logic duplication in a correctness-sensitive area.[1]

32. `executeinvm(...)` always attempts to delete the session in `finally`, so post-failure forensic inspection and manual recovery become impossible even when preserving the failed environment would be the correct behavior.[1]

33. `instavm.createsession(timeoutseconds=300)` hardcodes a short session timeout in the execution path, which is a functional mismatch for tasks that legitimately require long runtime.[1]

34. `createvm(..., vmlifetimeseconds=300)` sets a five-minute default VM lifetime, which is another hard stop incompatible with durable autonomous execution.[1]

35. `SESSIONTTLSECONDS = 4 * 3600` expires chat/session state after four hours, so session continuity is shorter than the long-running orchestration behavior implied elsewhere.[1]

36. `MAXSESSIONS = 1000` exists alongside TTL-based session eviction logic, but the architecture shown stores session data in process memory guarded by `sessionslock`, so horizontal scaling and multi-process consistency are broken by design.[1]

37. In-memory globals such as `sessions`, `sessionaccesstimes`, and robot state protected by thread locks mean process restarts and multi-worker deployments can lose or diverge live state despite the presence of a persistent job store.[1]

38. `runasyncsync(...)` creates a brand-new event loop in a plain thread for each dispatch path, which is costly and can complicate cleanup because it does not explicitly shut down async generators or executor resources.[1]

39. `historysummary` is built inside the sync dispatch worker path but the extracted code shows no subsequent use of that value, which is dead work on a hot path.[1]

40. The orchestration flow mixes queue-based streaming, background threads, in-memory state, retry loops, and persistent jobs without a single explicit lease/heartbeat mechanism, so ownership of long-running work is not robustly coordinated after disconnects or restarts.[1]

41. The retry logic in several places uses increasing sleeps but no classification between transient infrastructure errors and deterministic logical errors, so many programmer bugs will be retried pointlessly instead of being surfaced immediately.[1]

42. `executeinvm(...)` retries session creation and execution several times but returns stringified error blobs such as `json.dumps(sess)` or raw exception text as pseudo-results, which blurs the boundary between machine-readable execution output and failure metadata.[1]

43. In `executetaskwithretry(...)`, verifier-driven script rewriting feeds the next attempt directly from model output, so a bad verifier response can replace a previously better script without any structural validation beyond execution outcome.[1]

44. The verifier path returns `False, script` after repeated verifier failures, which means the outer loop keeps working with an uncorrected script and can continue cycling indefinitely on the same failure pattern.[1]

45. The extracted code shows multiple comments and control paths explicitly describing “infinite retry loop never gives up,” which confirms the absence of a proper terminal error policy in core task execution.[1]

46. `taskcontext` stores only `message` text from prior results, so any rich execution artifacts, structured values, or machine-usable metadata are discarded before dependent tasks run.[1]

47. The swarm execution batches depend on `dependencies` filtered by `if d in validids`, so references to nonexistent dependency IDs are silently ignored rather than treated as graph-definition errors.[1]

48. Ignoring nonexistent dependency IDs in `toposorttasks(...)` can cause a malformed graph to run as though the missing prerequisite had already been satisfied.[1]

49. The persistent and in-memory state layers are not shown as transactionally linked, so a crash between emitting queue events, mutating memory, and saving job state can leave the system in inconsistent recovery state.[1]

50. The extracted orchestration design relies heavily on implicit string conventions like `status`, `message`, and event names rather than typed result objects, which makes cross-component contracts fragile and increases the chance of silent schema drift bugs.[1]

51. `_dispatch_council_sync(...)` buffers every emitted chunk into a Python list before returning, so long runs scale memory with the full nested transcript instead of streaming incrementally.[1]

52. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` has the same full-buffering behavior, which means large nested SWARM runs accumulate all events in memory before the outer generator can replay them.[1]

53. Nested `council` and `swarm` progress is not streamed live to the client, because `agentic_stream(...)` only yields the nested chunks after `_dispatch_*_sync(...)` has already finished.[1]

54. `ev_q.get()` in both dispatcher loops blocks forever with no timeout, so a wedged worker can stall the caller indefinitely.[1]

55. `t.join()` is called without a timeout in both dispatchers, so a deadlocked or hung worker thread can hang the request path forever.[1]

56. Both dispatchers use an unbounded `queue.Queue()`, so a fast producer and slow consumer can grow memory without any backpressure.[1]

57. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(task, session_id, history)` accepts `session_id` but never uses it, so the function signature advertises stateful behavior that the implementation ignores.[1]

58. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` computes `history_summary` and then never uses it, which is dead work on a hot path.[1]

59. `_dispatch_council_sync(...)` returns `result_holder[0] or ""`, which masks valid falsy results such as `0`, `False`, or an intentionally empty structured payload.[1]

60. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` uses the same `result_holder[0] or ""` pattern and therefore has the same falsy-result masking bug.[1]

61. `_run_async_sync(...)` closes the event loop directly without an explicit `shutdown_asyncgens()`, so async generator cleanup is not handled rigorously.[1]

62. `_run_async_sync(...)` also does not explicitly shut down any default executor resources attached to the loop before closing it.[1]

63. `agentic_stream(...)` retries the model call inside `while not model_call_ok:` with no hard retry cap, so a permanent upstream failure can loop forever.[1]

64. `full_assistant_response` is appended token by token before the streamed model turn has actually completed successfully, so partial failed generations contaminate the final answer state.[1]

65. When a streamed model call fails mid-turn, already-yielded tokens are not retracted from the client stream, so the user can see partial text from an attempt that is later retried.[1]

66. On retry, `full_assistant_response` is not rolled back, so partial text from failed attempts can be duplicated or interleaved into the final output.[1]

67. `delta_text_this_turn` is reset on retry, but the client has already received the previous partial tokens, so server-side state and client-visible state can diverge.[1]

68. `tool_calls_accumulated` is reset on retry, but the previous partial response was already emitted, so the replayed model call is no longer aligned with what the user saw.[1]

69. In the `council` path, `final_text` is appended to both the tool message and `full_assistant_response`, which mixes internal tool output into the assistant’s final text buffer.[1]

70. In the `swarm` path, `final_text` is appended the same way, so nested SWARM output is treated both as tool content and as assistant content.[1]

71. `agentic_stream(...)` stops only when there are no tool calls or when `MAX_TOOL_ROUNDS` is exhausted, but it does not emit a specific exhaustion error when the round cap is hit.[1]

72. `outcome["completed"] = bool(full_assistant_response)` treats any non-empty partial text as success even if the run actually terminated in an incomplete state.[1]

73. `yield sse_event("done", {})` runs unconditionally at the end of `agentic_stream(...)`, so the terminal event does not distinguish success from degraded completion.[1]

74. If tool-call arguments fail to parse, the code silently falls back to `{}`, which can turn malformed tool invocations into incorrect default-argument executions.[1]

75. Falling back to `{}` after tool-argument parse failure also destroys the original error context that would have made the failure actionable.[1]

76. Any unknown `fn_name` falls through to `dispatch_instavm_tool(...)`, so unsupported tool names are conflated with InstaVM operations instead of being rejected explicitly.[1]

77. The `exa_search` branch does not validate that `query` is non-empty before dispatching the search.[1]

78. The code appends tool messages using `tc["id"]` without validating that a usable tool-call ID was actually constructed.[1]

79. `tool_calls_accumulated[idx]["id"] += tc.id` assumes tool IDs arrive as incremental fragments, so repeated full IDs can be concatenated into corrupted identifiers.[1]

80. `tool_calls_accumulated[idx]["function"]["name"] += tc.function.name` makes the same risky concatenation assumption for function names.[1]

81. Tool-call accumulation assumes chunks arrive in a safe order by `index`, but there is no defensive validation if the transport or SDK delivers fragments unexpectedly.[1]

82. `current_messages` keeps growing by appending full tool outputs and assistant turns every round, which creates unbounded context growth across long loops.[1]

83. Large `result_str` values from tools are inserted back into `current_messages` without truncation or summarization, which can explode prompt size and slow later rounds.[1]

84. Tool errors are converted into JSON strings stored as plain tool content, so later model turns must infer structured error state from escaped text instead of a typed object.[1]

85. `phase_classify(...)` routes to `"swarm"` whenever `"swarm"` appears anywhere in the classifier output, so phrases like “not swarm” still misroute to swarm.[1]

86. `phase_classify(...)` has the same substring-routing problem for `"council"`, so negated or descriptive prose can be misclassified.[1]

87. If the classifier output is empty or ambiguous, short requests are forced to `"fast"` purely by message length instead of task complexity.[1]

88. If the classifier output is empty or ambiguous, long requests are forced to `"council"` by length alone, even when they actually require `"swarm"`.[1]

89. `phase_classify(...)` retries forever on repeated exceptions, so a persistent classifier failure can block routing indefinitely.[1]

90. `phase_classify(...)` truncates history to only the last four messages and 150 characters each, which can remove the very context needed for accurate routing.[1]

91. `phase_plan(...)` accepts whatever `json.loads(raw)` returns as a DAG without validating the schema before later phases index into it.[1]

92. The fenced-code extraction in `phase_plan(...)` uses naive `split(...)` logic, so multiple fenced blocks can cause it to select the wrong segment.[1]

93. `phase_plan(...)` does not verify that the parsed DAG contains a list under `"tasks"` before later code depends on that shape.[1]

94. `phase_plan(...)` does not verify that each task has required keys such as `"id"`, so later direct indexing can fail with avoidable `KeyError`s.[1]

95. The fallback DAG in `phase_plan(...)` hardcodes `"language": "python"`, which is semantically wrong for non-code tasks and non-Python tasks.[1]

96. The fallback DAG also truncates the goal to `message[:200]`, which throws away potentially critical objective detail at the planning boundary.[1]

97. `_parse_exec_result(...)` only tries the whole stdout and then the last non-empty line, so valid JSON on earlier lines is ignored unless the regex rescue path happens to find it.[1]

98. `_parse_exec_result(...)` uses a flat-brace regex that cannot parse nested JSON objects containing `"status"`, so valid structured results can be missed.[1]

99. `_parse_exec_result(...)` returns the first regex match it can decode, so an earlier stale status block can beat the final execution result.[1]

100. `_topo_sort(...)` silently ignores dependency IDs that are not present in `valid_ids`, so malformed DAGs are normalized instead of rejected.[1]

101. `_topo_sort(...)` directly indexes `t["id"]`, so malformed planner output crashes later instead of being rejected during DAG validation.[1]

102. `_topo_sort(...)` never checks for duplicate task IDs, so duplicate IDs collapse inside `valid_ids` and `completed`, breaking dependency semantics.[1]

103. `_topo_sort(...)` assumes `dependencies` is a proper iterable of task IDs, so a string dependency would be iterated character by character.[1]

104. `_topo_sort(...)` removes tasks from `remaining` using `list.remove(...)` inside a loop, which gives it avoidable quadratic behavior on larger DAGs.[1]

105. When `_topo_sort(...)` detects no schedulable batch, it does `batch = list(remaining)` instead of raising a cycle error, so dependency cycles are executed rather than rejected.[1]

106. After that cycle fallback, `_topo_sort(...)` marks all remaining tasks as completed even though their prerequisites were never actually satisfied.[1]

107. `_worker_model_for(task_id)` assigns models from `md5(task_id)`, so scheduling depends on arbitrary task identifiers rather than task requirements or model suitability.[1]

108. Because `_worker_model_for(...)` keys on `task_id`, trivial planner renumbering can change model assignment without changing task meaning.[1]

109. `_dispatch_council_sync(...)` and `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` duplicate nearly the same thread/queue orchestration logic, which increases defect-fix drift risk.[1]

110. The queue-based nested-dispatch design stores every intermediate event twice, once in `ev_q` and once in `chunks`, which doubles memory pressure for large nested runs.[1]

111. Both dispatcher workers rely on `ev_q.put(None)` in `finally`, so if the process dies before `finally` executes the consumer can block forever waiting for a sentinel.[1]

112. Both dispatchers create a per-run task directory but do not return its path to the caller, which makes later inspection, cleanup, and correlation harder than necessary.[1]

113. `sse_event(...)` encodes the event type inside the JSON payload instead of using SSE’s native `event:` field, so the stream uses custom framing where standard SSE semantics would be simpler.[1]

114. `_parse_sse(...)` only understands the custom single-line `data: ...` format and is not a general SSE parser.[1]

115. `_parse_sse(...)` strips the entire chunk before parsing, so concatenated or multi-event chunks are not handled safely.[1]

116. `_parse_sse(...)` swallows JSON parse failures and returns `None`, which makes malformed upstream events disappear silently.[1]

117. `agentic_stream(...)` uses synchronous `time.sleep(...)` for backoff, which blocks the streaming worker thread instead of using cooperative waiting.[1]

118. The warning text emitted from `agentic_stream(...)` is hardcoded in Hungarian, so those warning events are not language-consistent with arbitrary input languages.[1]

119. The `phase_classify(...)` docstring says the model decides among fast, council, and swarm, but the implementation overrides ambiguous outputs with hardcoded length heuristics, so the model is not actually the sole router.[1]

120. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` computes `history_summary` but never feeds it into `phase_plan(...)`, `phase_swarm(...)`, or `phase_aggregate(...)`, so the work is both dead and misleading.[1]

121. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` exposes `session_id` in the signature without using it anywhere in the function body, which is an implementation-signature mismatch.[1]

122. `_dispatch_council_sync(...)` stores worker exceptions in `exc_holder` and only raises after the queue loop and `join()`, so failure signaling is delayed until after waiting.[1]

123. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` has the same delayed-failure pattern, which can postpone error propagation until long after the actual failure occurred.[1]

124. `agentic_stream(...)` stores assistant content as `delta_text_this_turn or None`, so a tool-call-only turn gets a `None` payload instead of a stable empty string shape.[1]

125. Tool failure payloads are serialized with `json.dumps(...)` and inserted into the conversation as plain text, which forces later model turns to reverse-parse error structure from text.[1]

126. In the `exa_search` path, the human-facing stream receives `sources` events while the model-facing history receives only `result_str`, so the two views of the same tool run are structurally inconsistent.[1]

127. In both nested-tool paths, `final_text` is used simultaneously as the tool output and as assistant output, which blurs role boundaries in the transcript.[1]

128. If `council` returns an empty string, the placeholder `"(council returned no response)"` is fed into model history as if it were meaningful tool content.[1]

129. If `swarm` returns an empty string, the placeholder `"(swarm returned no result)"` is likewise fed into model history as if it were factual output.[1]

130. When tool dispatch raises, the loop appends an error tool message and continues rather than deciding whether the overall run should abort, so broken tool cycles can consume all tool rounds pointlessly.[1]

131. `outcome["completed"]` depends only on whether `full_assistant_response` is non-empty, so a tool-only successful run with no assistant text is marked incomplete.[1]

132. The same completion rule means a run with only partial pre-failure assistant text can be marked complete even when the requested work never finished.[1]

133. `sse_event(...)` does not produce deterministic key ordering in its JSON payloads, so snapshot-style tests of emitted SSE text are unnecessarily brittle.[1]

134. `_run_async_sync(...)` sets the new loop as the thread’s current event loop and never restores any previous loop reference, which makes nested reuse patterns more fragile.[1]

135. The design launches a new OS thread for each nested `council` or `swarm` dispatch instead of using a reusable pool, which adds avoidable thread churn under bursty workloads.[1]

136. `phase_plan(...)` converts a planner failure into a silent single-task fallback after three attempts, so a major planning error is downgraded to a simpler execution path without a hard stop.[1]

137. That single-task fallback can radically change task semantics, because it replaces the planner’s decomposition with one generic “Execute task” step.[1]

138. `phase_plan(...)` does not validate dependency references before they are handed to `_topo_sort(...)`, so graph errors are deferred into weaker downstream behavior.[1]

139. `_topo_sort(...)` constructs `valid_ids` before checking for duplicates or invalid task objects, so malformed graph state is normalized too early.[1]

140. `_worker_model_for(...)` computes a full MD5 digest on every scheduling decision even though it only needs a stable partition, which is unnecessary overhead for a hot routing helper.[1]

141. `_parse_exec_result(...)` only accepts JSON objects and ignores other valid machine-readable result shapes such as arrays, so structured outputs outside that narrow shape are discarded.[1]

142. `_parse_exec_result(...)` prioritizes whole-stdout parsing, so any log prefix invalidates an otherwise valid final JSON document unless the last-line or regex rescue happens to recover it.[1]

143. `_dispatch_swarm_sync(...)` does not pass session state or history summary into `phase_swarm(...)` or `phase_aggregate(...)`, so later phases operate with less context than the function signature suggests.[1]

144. Both dispatchers create task directories with `exist_ok=True`, which suppresses collision errors instead of enforcing uniqueness if a directory name clash ever occurs.[1]

145. Both dispatcher workers place only a sentinel into the queue on completion and do not emit a dedicated terminal status event, so the outer stream cannot distinguish clean completion from exception completion until after thread join.[1]

146. Because nested chunks are replayed only after nested completion, the client can sit idle for a long time even though progress events are being produced internally.[1]

147. That idle buffering behavior makes the SSE connection vulnerable to intermediary idle timeouts during legitimate long-running nested work.[1]

148. `phase_classify(...)` lowercases and strips punctuation from the raw response but never validates it against an allowed set of exact tokens, so arbitrary prose is forced through substring heuristics.[1]

149. The classifier’s final fallback is pure message-length logic, which is a brittle proxy for complexity, tool need, and execution mode.[1]

150. The combination of infinite classifier retry, buffered nested dispatch, and blocking queue waits creates several separate no-progress states where the system can appear alive but make no externally visible forward progress.[1]
